To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) systemic LPS pre‐ and post‐conditioning reduce leukocyte infiltration into the injured central nervous tissue and thus limit blood–brain/spinal cord barrier breakdown and neuronal cell death.
the systemic administration of LPS, which mimics the systemic response to acute brain injury, reduces the inflammatory response in the injured central nervous systems of rats.

(i) intravenous LPS pre‐ or post‐conditioning reduces the inflammatory infiltrates in the brain and spinal cord after injury; (ii) the reduction in inflammatory infiltrate was associated with a reduced breakdown of the blood‐brain barrier and blood‐spinal cord barrier; and (iii) LPS‐induced pre‐ or post conditioning is more effective in reducing the inflammatory infiltrate than IL‐1β‐induced pre conditioning.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the brain and the spinal cord respond to injury.
the mechanisms by which leukocytes are mobilized and recruited to the injured central nervous tissue and the consequences of this inflammatory response.

the role of inflammatory mediators in the pathophysiology of traumatic brain injury and the potential use of pro‐inflammatory mediators as neuroprotective agents in the treatment of brain and spinal cord injury.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the systemic response is not necessarily detrimental, but can be beneficial, depending on its timing and the type and severity of the insult.
the systemic inflammatory response to injury may have a beneficial effect on the outcome of acute CNS injury, which could be used to advantage in the clinical setting.

the use of lipopolysacharide (LPS) in a pre or post conditioning manner can reduce the inflammatory infiltrate in the injured brain and/or spinal cord, which is a potentially neuroprotective treatment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
systemic LPS conditioning can protect the injured central nerve system from the damaging effects of leukocyte recruitment.
LPS pre‐ or post‐conditioning is a novel therapeutic strategy that may be effective in limiting secondary damage in acute brain or spinal cord injury.

the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) is an important component of the pathophysiology of acute brain injury, and that the use of LPS as a pro‐inflammatory preconditioning agent is neuroprotective.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the systemic response to injury is a major contributor to the outcome and that the timing of the intervention is crucial.
systemic LPS pre‐treatment reduces the number of neutrophils recruited to the brain after intracranial hemorrhage.
systemic LPS pre‐ and post‐conditioning can limit the inflammatory response to brain injury.
